newsitem.title: USA: BRAZIL TRADE GAP NO DEVALUATION SIGNAL-US ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL TRADE GAP NO DEVALUATION SIGNAL-US ANALYSTS.

text.p: Further widening of Brazil's trade deficit may prompt import curbs, but the July surge in the trade gap does not signal a near term devaluation of the real, U.S. analysts said.
On Tuesday, Brazil reported an $811 million trade deficit for July, compared with economists' forecasts for a figure nearer $500 million.

While special factors may have influenced the July data, Brazil officials remain sensitive to the monetary situation and would likely tap the economic brakes if the deficit worsens, U.S. experts said.

"If the deficit is widening to too great an extent, that is going to prompt action by the government on fronts other than the currency front," said Larry Krohn, a Latin America economist at UBS Securities.
Brazil's foreign exchange reserves rose in July, so the deficit spike should not add to fears of speculative currency attacks or an official devaluation, Krohn said.
A more likely outcome, however, would be a government tightening of consumer credit in order to slow domestic demand, analysts said.

"Aside from using a little bit of reserves and jawboning the market, I think the only thing they can do is tighten credit conditions," said Jaime Valdivia, senior Latin America analyst at Morgan Stanley.
In the past, Brazil has shortened the repayment period for credit card purchases of foreign products or raised the country's Basic Interest Rate (TBC).
Either method would slow imports of consumer items without cutting into spending on capital goods, which can have long-run economic benefits, UBS's Krohn said.
But some analysts have noticed a shift in Brazil's monetary tactics toward the supply side.
Peter Greenbaum, a Latin America economist at Smith Barney, said Brazil might be inclined to reduce the number of capital goods that are exempted from import tariffs.
"We've already seen the economic team moving in the direction of supply-side management," he said.
The economists agreed, however, there would be no change in the current exchange rate regime, at least not until the 1998 elections.
"There's no doubt the currency is overvalued, but the question is, what do they gain by devaluing it ... in front of an election?" Greenbaum said.
Brazil's cash foreign exchange reserves rose $2.8 billion to a record $59.5 billion in July, making an attack on the real less likely.
Morgan Stanley's Valdivia estimated Brazil maintains reserves equal to between eight and nine months' worth of goods and services imports.
"They have the firepower to face a speculative attack," he said."
Brazil lowered its real/dollar trading band by 0.9 percent on Tuesday, causing the real to fall to 1.0840 per dollar. Analysts called the move routine and said it had no policy implications.
